content: The health benefits of breastfeeding are widely recognized, but there is significant debate regarding the optimal duration of exclusive breastfeeding. Since 2001, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life. However, in developed countries, much of the discussion has focused on whether this practice provides adequate micronutrient intake and the extent of its health benefits. The objective of this review was to compare the effects of exclusive breastfeeding for six months versus exclusive breastfeeding for three to four months followed by mixed feeding (the introduction of complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding) until six months. The outcomes assessed included child health, growth, and development, as well as maternal health. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted, including The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, BIOSIS, African Index Medicus, IMEMR, and LILACS. The search covered studies published between January 2007 and June 2011, and additional studies were identified through expert contacts. The initial review in 2000 identified 2,668 unique citations, while an updated review in 2006 yielded 835 additional citations. The review included all internally controlled clinical trials and observational studies that compared health outcomes in infants exclusively breastfed for six months or more versus those exclusively breastfed for at least three to four months with continued mixed breastfeeding until six months. Studies were categorized based on design (controlled trials versus observational studies), geographic setting (developing versus developed countries), and timing of feeding comparisons (three to seven months versus later). A total of 23 studies met the inclusion criteria, including 11 from developing countries (two of which were controlled trials conducted in Honduras) and 12 from developed countries (all observational studies). Definitions of exclusive breastfeeding varied significantly across studies. The findings indicated that neither the controlled trials nor the observational studies showed evidence of deficits in weight or length gain among infants exclusively breastfed for six months. However, larger sample sizes would be needed to rule out small differences in the risk of undernutrition. In developing countries, where newborn iron stores may be suboptimal, exclusive breastfeeding without iron supplementation for six months could negatively affect hematologic status. A study from Belarus found no significant benefits of six months of exclusive breastfeeding (compared to three months of exclusive breastfeeding followed by mixed feeding) on height, weight, body mass index, dental health, cognitive ability, or behavior at 6.5 years of age. However, studies from Belarus, Iran, and Nigeria demonstrated that infants exclusively breastfed for six months or more had a significantly lower risk of gastrointestinal infections. Additionally, studies from Iran and Nigeria showed a reduced risk of respiratory infections in these infants. No significant reduction in the risk of atopic conditions, such as eczema or asthma, was observed in studies conducted in Finland, Australia, and Belarus. Data from two trials in Honduras and observational studies in Bangladesh and Senegal suggested that exclusive breastfeeding for six months was associated with delayed resumption of menstruation in mothers and, in the Honduran trials, more rapid postpartum weight loss. In conclusion, infants exclusively breastfed for six months experience a lower risk of gastrointestinal infections compared to those partially breastfed from three or four months onward. No deficits in growth have been observed in infants exclusively breastfed for six months or longer in either developing or developed countries. Additionally, mothers of these infants benefit from prolonged lactational amenorrhea. While individual management of infants is essential to address any growth concerns or adverse outcomes, the evidence supports the general recommendation of exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life in both developing and developed settings.
